why: The passage says yields are lower, so per-hectare earnings are not guaranteed.
Slower ripening under shade produces denser beans.
The text says shade lowers yields.
items.explanation: Quality and price rise while volume falls, creating a trade-off.

items.passage: Honey often contains pollen grains from the flowers the bees visited. Because pollen grains have distinctive shapes, a sample can reveal which plants were in bloom. Analysis of a jar from a market stall showed pollen from a plant that flowers only in early spring, several months before the honey was sold. The jar was probably not from the most recent harvest.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Pollen can date honey by showing which flowering season produced it.
wrongs: Pollen analysis cannot distinguish one season's honey from another's.
The jar was certainly made from artificial honey.
Bees visit only one plant species in a season.
why: Distinctive pollen tied to a season is exactly what enables dating.
The passage infers age, not adulteration.
The passage describes pollen from visited flowers generally.
items.explanation: Season-specific pollen in a jar sold later points to an earlier harvest.

items.passage: Shipworms bore into wooden hulls and pilings, digesting the wood with the help of bacteria. A hull recovered from a cold, low-oxygen harbour showed far less damage than one from a warm estuary. Conservators now store excavated timbers in tanks where oxygen is limited, because the animals that attack wood need oxygen as well as wood.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Limiting oxygen slows the organisms that would otherwise consume waterlogged wood.
wrongs: Warm water protects wood from shipworms.
Shipworms digest wood without the help of bacteria.
Oxygen has no effect on wood-boring animals.
why: The warm estuary showed more damage.
The passage mentions bacterial help.
The storage method relies on oxygen limitation.
items.explanation: The comparison and the storage practice both turn on oxygen.

items.passage: A solar still collects drinking water by evaporating brine under a transparent cover and condensing the vapour on the underside. Output depends on sunlight and on the area of the cover. On a cloudy day a small still may produce only a few spoonfuls, while a larger still in full sun produces liters. The device is therefore a supplement rather than a stand-alone supply.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: A solar still's output is too weather-dependent to guarantee water on its own.
wrongs: A solar still produces the same output in all weather.
Small stills outperform large ones in full sun.
Condensation reduces the amount of water collected.
why: The passage describes output varying with sunlight and area.
Larger stills in full sun produce liters.
Condensation is the collection step.
items.explanation: Variable output under clouds explains why the device is a supplement.

items.passage: Fish ferment faster in warm weather, and salt slows the process. Communities that live where temperatures stay high use more salt in their preserved fish than communities in cooler regions. A recipe that works in one place can therefore fail in another, not because the method is wrong but because the conditions have changed.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Preservation recipes have to be adjusted to local temperature.
wrongs: Salt speeds fermentation in warm weather.
Cooler regions require more salt than warmer ones.
A recipe that works in one region always works in another.
why: Salt slows fermentation.
The passage says warmer communities use more salt.
The passage says a recipe can fail when conditions change.
items.explanation: Temperature changes the rate of fermentation, so salt amounts must adapt.

items.passage: A cathedral bell is tuned by grinding metal from its rim. Removing material lowers the pitch and can also change the relationships among the bell's partial tones. Founders therefore remove metal in small stages, testing between each. A bell ground too far cannot be restored, because the metal cannot be added back.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Tuning is irreversible, so it proceeds cautiously and in measured steps.
wrongs: Founders grind the rim quickly because extra metal can be added later.
Grinding raises the pitch of a bell.
Partial tones are unaffected by removing metal.
why: Metal cannot be added back.
The passage says removing material lowers pitch.
Grinding can change the partial relationships.
items.explanation: Irreversibility explains the incremental method.

items.passage: Compacted soil resists root growth even when it holds enough water. Roots follow pores and cracks, and compaction closes those channels. In a field where machinery has passed repeatedly, roots may spread sideways above a hard layer instead of reaching deeper moisture. The plants survive but depend on rain in the upper soil.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Compaction makes crops more vulnerable to drought in the upper soil.
wrongs: Compaction helps roots reach deeper water.
Roots grow through compacted soil more easily than through pores.
Machinery traffic improves the soil's pore structure.
why: Roots are blocked from deeper layers.
Roots follow pores, which compaction closes.
Traffic is the cause of the compaction described.
items.explanation: Shallow rooting ties survival to upper-soil moisture.

items.passage: Soot deposits on cave ceilings accumulate in thin layers that record the fires below. A layer rich in charcoal indicates a larger or more frequent fire; a gap indicates a period without burning. Archaeologists reading a sequence of layers can therefore reconstruct how often people used a cave, even when no tools survive.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Soot layers provide a record of human activity independent of artefacts.
wrongs: Soot layers form only when a cave is empty of people.
A gap in the layers proves that the cave was never visited.
Charcoal-rich layers indicate cold weather rather than fires.
why: The passage says the layers record use.
A gap indicates a period without burning, not no visits.
Charcoal richness tracks fire size or frequency.
items.explanation: Burning evidence alone can show occupation frequency.

items.passage: Harbour sediment traps lead, copper and organic matter washed from streets and ships. A core taken near a former shipyard contains a sharp peak in copper at the depth corresponding to the yard's busiest decades. Above that layer, concentrations fall as the yard closed and runoff was diverted. The core therefore reads as a history of industrial activity.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Chemical layers in harbour mud can be tied to the rise and fall of nearby industry.
wrongs: Copper concentrations rise after the shipyard closed.
Harbour sediment carries no trace of industrial activity.
The peak in copper came from natural erosion only.
why: Concentrations fall above the peak as the yard closed.
The passage describes clear traces.
The peak corresponds to the yard's busiest decades.
items.explanation: The copper profile matches the yard's timeline.

items.passage: Bats that hibernate through winter need high humidity as well as steady cold. Dry air draws water from their skin and wings, and an aroused bat burns fat it cannot replace until spring. A cave that is cold but draughty can therefore be worse for a colony than one that is slightly warmer but still.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Stable, humid conditions matter more to hibernating bats than cold alone.
wrongs: Warm, dry caves are ideal for hibernating bats.
Bats can replace fat easily during winter.
Air movement has no effect on hibernating bats.
why: Dry air causes water loss and arousal.
The passage says fat cannot be replaced until spring.
Draughty caves are described as harmful.
items.explanation: Humidity and stillness protect the fat reserve that must last the winter.

items.passage: Roof tiles are laid so that each row overlaps the one below. Water running down the slope crosses from one tile to the next without reaching the deck beneath. If the overlap is too small, wind-driven rain can be forced upward under the edge. The overlap is therefore a specification, not a decorative choice.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Overlap width must be set to withstand the weather a roof will face.
wrongs: A smaller overlap gives better protection in strong wind.
Water runs upward across the roof under normal conditions.
The overlap has no effect on whether rain reaches the deck.
why: Too small an overlap lets wind-driven rain under the edge.
Water runs down the slope; only driven rain moves upward.
The overlap determines whether water crosses safely.
items.explanation: Weather exposure sets the minimum overlap.

items.passage: Some plants rely on ants to carry their seeds. The seed carries a fleshy appendage that ants eat, and the seed itself is discarded underground. Seeds moved this way end up buried, where they escape drying and some seed-eaters. The plant pays a small food cost for dispersal and burial.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: The food reward buys the seed both transport and a safer place to germinate.
wrongs: Ants destroy the seeds they carry.
The appendage prevents ants from moving the seed.
Seeds left on the surface survive better than buried ones.
why: The seed is discarded intact underground.
The appendage is the reward that attracts ants.
Burial is described as protection.
items.explanation: Transport plus burial explains the benefit of the food cost.

items.passage: Clipper ships carried tea from China to London, and speed mattered because early arrivals sold at higher prices. Their hulls were narrow and their sail area large, which made them fast in strong winds but hard to handle in a calm. After steamships offered reliable schedules, the clippers lost their advantage.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Reliability of arrival proved more valuable than the fastest possible passage.
wrongs: Clippers remained the fastest option after steamships appeared.
Calm weather was the clippers' greatest advantage.
Speed had no effect on the price tea fetched.
why: Clippers lost their advantage to steamships.
The narrow hull was hard to handle in a calm.
The passage says early arrivals sold higher.
items.explanation: Steam's dependable schedule displaced the clipper's speed premium.

items.passage: Some birds lay eggs with thinner shells where the soil is low in calcium. The birds cannot manufacture calcium, so they must take it from food or grit. Studies of a population on calcium-poor ground found thinner shells and more breakages than in a population on limestone. The difference tracked geology, not species.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Access to calcium in the environment shapes shell thickness in these birds.
wrongs: Shell thickness is fixed by the species and cannot vary.
Calcium-poor soil produces thicker shells.
Birds can synthesise calcium without eating it.
why: The two populations differ within the same species.
Thin shells occur on poor ground.
The passage says birds must obtain calcium from food or grit.
items.explanation: The geologic contrast, with the same species, isolates calcium availability.

items.passage: Residue inside Roman amphorae can be identified by its chemical signature. Jars found in a storage room contained traces of olive oil, while jars from a nearby shop contained fish sauce. The two sets were the same shape. Shape alone therefore does not tell an archaeologist what a vessel carried.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Contents must be identified chemically, because form does not reveal use.
wrongs: Amphora shape reliably indicates what was stored inside.
Fish sauce and olive oil leave identical residues.
All jars in a storage room held the same product.
why: Identical shapes held different contents.
The distinction comes from chemical signatures.
The passage contrasts two nearby sets.
items.explanation: Same shape, different contents forces chemical identification.

items.passage: Pencil leads are graded by hardness, which depends on the ratio of graphite to clay. More clay makes a harder lead that holds a sharp point and prints lightly; more graphite makes a softer lead that darkens the page and wears quickly. A drafter choosing a lead is choosing between precision and darkness.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: No single lead suits both fine detail and dense shading equally well.
wrongs: Hard leads darken the page more than soft leads.
Clay increases the darkness of a pencil line.
The graphite-to-clay ratio has no effect on wear.
why: Hard leads print lightly; soft leads darken.
Graphite provides darkness, not clay.
The ratio determines both darkness and wear.
items.explanation: The trade-off between point retention and darkness is the basis of the grading scale.

items.passage: A bleached coral reef can recover if the algae that live inside the coral return while the coral is still alive. Recovery is slower where the reef is also stressed by sediment or warm water. Surveys find that reefs with cleaner water regain color sooner after a bleaching event than reefs near river mouths.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Reducing local stress helps a reef recover from bleaching.
wrongs: Sediment speeds the return of algae to coral.
Bleached coral is always dead and cannot recover.
Warm water improves recovery after bleaching.
why: Cleaner-water reefs recovered sooner.
The passage describes recovery while the coral is alive.
Warm water is named as an additional stress.
items.explanation: The comparison points to local stress as a brake on recovery.

items.passage: Salmon that die after spawning leave carcasses in streams. Their bodies carry nitrogen from the ocean, which enters the food web as the carcasses decay. Trees along a stream with many spawning salmon contain more marine-derived nitrogen than trees along a stream without them. The forest is therefore linked to the ocean by the fish.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Marine nutrients reach streamside forests through the bodies of spawning fish.
wrongs: Trees cannot take up nitrogen from decaying fish.
Salmon remove nitrogen from streamside forests.
The connection exists only in streams without spawning salmon.
why: The passage reports elevated nitrogen in those trees.
The carcasses add nitrogen.
The contrast is between streams with and without salmon.
items.explanation: The nitrogen signature in trees traces the marine source through the carcasses.

items.passage: A windmill's sails turn a shaft, and gearing converts that slow, powerful rotation into a faster one at the millstone. Changing the gear ratio changes the speed of the stone without changing the wind. Millers keep several gears on hand so that a strong wind and a light one can both be used.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Gearing lets a miller match the stone's speed to the available wind.
wrongs: Gearing changes the amount of wind reaching the sails.
A single fixed gear ratio suits every wind condition.
The millstone turns more slowly than the shaft in all gears.
why: Gearing converts rotation, not wind.
The passage describes changing ratios for different winds.
The gearing speeds the rotation up at the stone.
items.explanation: Multiple gears exist to keep stone speed steady across wind strengths.

items.passage: A manuscript written with acidic ink can lose text at the same time it loses paper. Washing a leaf removes acid but may also lift the ink, so conservators first test a small, unimportant area. If the ink survives the test, the leaf can be washed; if not, it is stored dry and digitised instead.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Treatment decisions depend on evidence from a test before the whole leaf is exposed.
wrongs: Every leaf can be washed safely with acidic ink.
Testing a small area damages the whole manuscript.
Digitisation removes acid from the paper.
why: Washing may lift the ink.
The test uses an unimportant area precisely to avoid damage.
Digitisation creates a copy; it does not treat the paper.
items.explanation: The small-area test governs whether the full treatment is safe.

items.passage: Moss on a stone wall is thickest on the side that receives the most moisture, not always the side that receives the most light. On a wall shaded by trees, moss may cover the whole face, while an exposed wall carries moss in a band near the ground. Anyone reading moss as a compass would need to know the local conditions.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Moss growth reflects moisture and shade, so it is an unreliable direction indicator without local context.
wrongs: Moss always grows on the north side of a wall regardless of shade.
Moss requires full sunlight and avoids damp surfaces.
A shaded wall carries less moss than an exposed one.
why: The passage says moisture matters more than direction.
Moss is thickest where moisture is greatest.
The shaded wall may be covered entirely.
items.explanation: Moisture and shade dominate, which defeats naive compass use.

items.passage: Volcanic lightning occurs in ash clouds when particles collide and separate charge. The effect is more common in eruptions that produce fine ash and vigorous convection. Observers have used lightning detection to track eruptions at night and in bad weather, when cameras see little. The electrical signal becomes a remote sensing tool.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Detecting lightning can reveal an eruption that visibility would hide.
wrongs: Volcanic lightning occurs only in eruptions with no ash.
Lightning detection replaces the need to monitor volcanoes.
Cameras see eruptions better at night than detectors do.
why: The passage ties lightning to fine ash and convection.
It is a tool, not a replacement for monitoring.
The text says cameras see little at night and in bad weather.
items.explanation: The electrical signal works when visual observation fails.

items.passage: Wool takes dye unevenly if its scales are damaged. Makers therefore clean fleece gently and avoid sudden temperature changes during dyeing, since a rapid shift can shock the fibres. A dye lot that looks patchy often records a handling error rather than a fault in the dye itself.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Even color depends on gentle handling as much as on the dye recipe.
wrongs: Rapid temperature changes improve the evenness of dye uptake.
Damaged scales help wool absorb dye uniformly.
Patchiness always indicates a faulty dye.
why: The passage warns that rapid shifts shock the fibres.
Damage is described as causing uneven uptake.
Patchiness often reflects handling, not the dye.
items.explanation: Handling errors, not the dye, explain many patchy lots.

items.passage: Charcoal in lake sediment comes from fires in the surrounding catchment. A layer with abundant charcoal often coincides with a shift from forest pollen to grass pollen. The two signals together suggest that fire removed trees and allowed grasses to spread. Neither signal alone would establish the sequence.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Combining charcoal and pollen evidence links fire to vegetation change.
wrongs: Charcoal layers indicate that no fire occurred in the catchment.
Pollen shifts always precede fires by several centuries.
Grass pollen excludes the possibility of fire.
why: Charcoal records fire.
The signals are described as coinciding.
Grass pollen follows fire in the proposed sequence.
items.explanation: The coincidence of the two proxies is what ties fire to the vegetation shift.

items.passage: A tea clipper's narrow hull reduced drag but also reduced cargo space. Owners packed light, high-value cargo such as tea and raced for the first market. When the Suez Canal opened, steamships could take a shorter route that sailing ships could not use reliably. The clippers' advantage narrowed.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: A route change reduced the value of the clippers' speed and small capacity.
wrongs: The Suez Canal made the clippers' route shorter than the steamships'.
Clippers carried bulk cargo more cheaply after the canal opened.
Narrow hulls increased cargo capacity.
why: Steamships took the shorter route the clippers could not use.
Clippers carried light, high-value cargo.
The passage says the narrow hull reduced capacity.
items.explanation: The canal favored steam, eroding the clipper's niche.

items.passage: A bell foundry casts a bell slightly larger than its final size because tuning removes metal. The founder also adjusts the profile so that the bell's partial tones form the intended chord. Changing the profile after casting is nearly impossible, so the shape must be right before the metal cools.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Most of a bell's tonal character is fixed at casting, with tuning only refining it.
wrongs: A bell's profile can be reshaped easily after casting.
Tuning adds metal to raise the pitch.
The partial tones are unrelated to the bell's shape.
why: The passage says reshaping after casting is nearly impossible.
Tuning removes metal.
The profile is adjusted to shape the partials.
items.explanation: Since profile cannot be changed later, the cast shape carries the tonal design.

items.passage: An oyster reef filters water as its inhabitants feed. A dense reef can clear suspended particles from a large volume in a day. When reefs were removed, water clarity fell and sunlight reached less deeply. Seagrasses, which need light, declined in the same estuaries.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Losing oyster reefs can reduce water clarity enough to harm seagrass.
wrongs: Oyster reefs increase suspended particles in the water.
Seagrasses grow better in turbid water.
Water clarity improved after reefs were removed.
why: The reef filters particles out.
Seagrass needs light, which turbidity blocks.
The passage says clarity fell.
items.explanation: Filtration loss, lower clarity and seagrass decline form the causal chain.

items.passage: A mudbrick wall shrinks as it dries. If the outer surface dries faster than the core, the difference in shrinkage pulls the surface apart. Builders therefore mix straw into the clay, which slows drying and gives the shrinking mass something to hold onto. The cracks that appear in unstrawed brick begin at the surface.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Straw reduces cracking by evening out the drying of a mudbrick.
wrongs: Straw speeds drying and increases surface shrinkage.
Mudbrick does not change size as it dries.
Cracks in unstrawed brick start at the core.
why: The passage says straw slows drying.
The wall shrinks as it dries.
The text says cracks begin at the surface.
items.explanation: Straw moderates the moisture gradient that causes surface cracking.

items.passage: Goats browse young trees before they can grow above reach. On islands where goats were removed, tree lines moved upslope within decades. On islands where goats remained, the same species stayed low and sparse. The difference between the islands tracks the presence of goats rather than climate.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Grazing animals can hold a tree line in place.
wrongs: Tree lines are determined entirely by temperature.
Removing goats prevented trees from spreading.
Goats help young trees grow above browsing height.
why: The paired islands share climate but differ in goats.
Tree lines moved upslope after removal.
Goats browse young trees before they escape reach.
items.explanation: The island comparison isolates grazing as the cause.

items.passage: Lichens absorb water and nutrients directly through their surfaces, which also means they absorb pollutants. A lichen transplanted from a clean site to a city center accumulates metals within months. Species differ in tolerance, so a survey of which lichens survive can map pollution without instruments.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Lichen communities can act as biological pollution monitors.
wrongs: Lichens filter out pollutants and remain unaffected.
All lichen species respond to pollution in the same way.
Transplanted lichens cannot accumulate metals.
why: The passage says they absorb pollutants.
Tolerance differs by species.
The transplant accumulated metals within months.
items.explanation: Absorption plus species-specific tolerance supports biomonitoring.

items.passage: Dredging records show how often a harbour was cleared. Sediment cores show layers of coarse material where dredging mixed the bed. Where the two records agree, historians can date a period of increased shipping. Where they disagree, one source is probably incomplete.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Agreement between independent records strengthens a claim about harbour use.
wrongs: Dredging records and sediment cores always agree.
Coarse sediment indicates that no dredging occurred.
Disagreement proves both records are correct.
why: The passage describes cases where they disagree.
Mixed beds leave coarse layers.
Disagreement is explained as incompleteness in one source.
items.explanation: Cross-checking two independent records is what supports the dating.

items.passage: In permafrost, ice wedges form when meltwater enters cracks and refreezes. Repeated widening pushes the surrounding ground upward and outward, creating patterned polygons at the surface. Where the climate warms, wedges melt and the polygons subside. The pattern is therefore a visible record of ground temperature.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Changing polygon patterns can signal thawing permafrost.
wrongs: Polygons form only where the ground never freezes.
Melting ice wedges raises the ground surface.
The patterns are unrelated to temperature.
why: Freezing meltwater is the mechanism.
Melting causes subsidence.
The passage links the pattern to ground temperature.
items.explanation: The surface pattern tracks the state of the ice wedges.

items.passage: A fresco is painted on wet lime plaster. As the plaster sets, the pigment becomes part of the wall, which is why the color lasts. The painter must work quickly, because once the plaster dries the surface will not accept pigment in the same way. Frescoes were therefore planned in sections sized to one day's work.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: The technique's durability depends on painting before the plaster sets.
wrongs: Fresco pigment sits on top of dry plaster.
A painter could return to the same section weeks later.
The sections were sized to the painter's arm length only.
why: The pigment becomes part of the wall as it sets.
Dry plaster will not accept pigment the same way.
Sections matched a day's work, not arm length.
items.explanation: The wet-plaster window explains both durability and the daily section plan.

items.passage: A bridge cable is protected from rust by a galvanised coating that corrodes before the steel beneath. The coating is sacrificial: it gives up metal so the cable does not. Once the coating is consumed, the steel begins to rust, so inspectors measure coating thickness rather than waiting for visible damage.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Measuring the protective layer gives earlier warning than looking for rust.
wrongs: Galvanising makes steel immune to corrosion.
Inspectors should ignore the coating and wait for rust.
The coating outlasts the steel it protects.
why: The coating corrodes so the steel does not.
By the time rust shows, the coating is gone.
Once consumed, the steel begins to rust.
items.explanation: Coating thickness is an early indicator of remaining protection.

items.passage: A fish's otolith grows in annual rings, much like a tree. The rings record the temperature and chemistry of the water the fish inhabited, and a single otolith carries the whole life history of one animal. Researchers can therefore place a fish in particular waters at particular ages, even after it has been caught far away.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Otoliths preserve a dated record of the environments a fish moved through.
wrongs: Otolith rings record only the fish's age, not its environment.
An otolith changes after the fish dies, erasing its history.
Otoliths grow without annual layers.
why: The rings record water chemistry as well as age.
The record survives in the recovered ear stone.
The passage describes annual rings.
items.explanation: Annual layers with environmental chemistry allow life-history reconstruction.

items.passage: In stony deserts, stones sometimes sit on pedestals of fine soil. Wind removes the loose material around a stone but cannot lift the stone itself, so the ground beneath it erodes more slowly. Over time the stone appears to rise. The pedestal is therefore a record of wind erosion, not of the stone being pushed upward.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: The surrounding ground has been lowered, leaving the stone elevated.
wrongs: The stone is gradually lifted by rising air currents.
Wind deposits soil beneath the stone.
Pedestals form only where the ground is fully protected from wind.
why: Deflation removes material around the stone.
The pedestal remains because erosion is slower beneath the stone.
Wind erosion is the mechanism, not protection.
items.explanation: Differential deflation lowers the surrounding plain.

items.passage: Many mushrooms fruit after rain, but rain alone is not enough. The mycelium must already have stored enough nutrients, and the air must cool enough to trigger development. A dry summer followed by a single storm often produces no flush, while a wet autumn with mild nights produces a large one.
items.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
items.correct: Fruiting depends on accumulated reserves and temperature as well as moisture.
wrongs: A single storm is sufficient to produce a mushroom flush.
Mushrooms fruit best in dry, warm conditions.
Mycelium stores no nutrients before fruiting.
why: The passage says rain alone is not enough.
Cooling nights and wet weather favor fruiting.
Reserves are described as necessary.
items.explanation: The passage names three conditions, not one.

items.passage: People often assume that a desert is empty of life because it looks bare. A closer look at a single square meter of sand can reveal seeds, dormant eggs and buried insects waiting for rain. Within days of a storm, the same ground may be covered with seedlings and insects that were invisible before.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It states a common assumption and then presents evidence that contradicts it.
wrongs: It lists several causes and ranks them by importance.
It describes a process step by step from beginning to end.
It compares two deserts and concludes that they are identical.
why: There is no ranking of causes.
No sequential process is described.
Only one setting is discussed.
items.explanation: The passage opens with an assumption, then offers hidden life as the correction.

items.passage: A hand loom and a power loom produce the same cloth, but they organize work differently. On a hand loom the weaver controls pace and pattern at every pass. A power loom fixes the pace and moves pattern control into the punch card or the computer. The change is less about speed than about where decisions sit.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain how mechanisation shifted control over pattern and pace away from the weaver.
wrongs: To argue that hand-woven cloth is of better quality.
To describe the technical steps of warping a loom.
To show that power looms produce no patterned cloth.
why: Quality is not compared.
Warping is never mentioned.
Pattern control is relocated, not eliminated.
items.explanation: The passage contrasts two looms and locates the real change in decision-making.

items.passage: Early maps of the ocean floor were assembled from lead lines dropped over the side. Each sounding gave one depth at one point. A century later, sonar surveyed whole swaths in a single pass. The difference is not merely accuracy: it is the shift from a scatter of points to a continuous surface.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It contrasts two surveying methods and explains what the change made possible.
wrongs: It narrates a single voyage in chronological order.
It lists the materials used to build sounding lines.
It argues that early maps were more accurate than sonar maps.
why: No voyage is described.
Materials are not listed.
Sonar is presented as the advance.
items.explanation: The passage juxtaposes lead-line and sonar surveys and names the conceptual gain.

items.passage: A paper conservator faced with a brittle volume has two options. Washing removes acid but risks the ink. Deacidification spray neutralises acid with less moisture but penetrates unevenly. The choice depends on the ink, the paper and how much time the collection can spare.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It presents two options, notes the risk of each, and says the choice is conditional.
wrongs: It recommends one treatment as correct in every case.
It describes the history of paper manufacture in order.
It explains why brittle paper cannot be treated at all.
why: The passage says the choice is conditional.
No manufacturing history is given.
Treatments are offered, not ruled out.
items.explanation: Two treatments, their risks, and conditional advice structure the passage.

items.passage: Bamboo is often called a grass, and the label matters. It grows from an underground rhizome, sends up hollow stems, and dies back after flowering. Each of these traits is shared with grasses and not with the trees it resembles. The resemblance to wood is a matter of size, not of family.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain why bamboo's botanical traits place it with grasses rather than trees.
wrongs: To argue that bamboo should be classified as a hardwood.
To describe how bamboo is harvested and dried.
To compare the strength of bamboo and steel.
why: The passage separates bamboo from trees.
Harvesting is not discussed.
No strength comparison appears.
items.explanation: Shared grass traits are the evidence behind the classification.

items.passage: A new bridge design was tested in a wind tunnel at increasing speeds. At low speeds the deck behaved as predicted. At a critical speed the deck began to twist, and the twisting grew instead of settling. The test was stopped, and the section was reshaped before the next run.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It narrates a test in sequence and ends with the response to a failure.
wrongs: It compares two bridge designs and declares one superior.
It explains the theory of wind loading without describing a test.
It lists several failures from different laboratories.
why: Only one design is tested.
A concrete test is described.
There is a single test sequence.
items.explanation: The passage follows the test from low speed to failure to redesign.

items.passage: Salt marshes absorb wave energy, store carbon and shelter young fish. They also migrate inland as sea level rises, but only if the land behind them is open. Where a seawall blocks that retreat, the marsh is squeezed against a hard edge and drowns. Protection therefore depends on what lies behind the marsh.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It lists benefits, introduces a condition for survival, and draws a conclusion about that condition.
wrongs: It describes the formation of salt marshes from bare mud.
It argues that seawalls are the best way to protect marshes.
It compares marshes in two countries and finds no difference.
why: Formation from mud is not described.
Seawalls are the obstacle in the example.
No country comparison appears.
items.explanation: Benefits, a migration condition, and the blocking seawall build to the conclusion.

items.passage: The claim that goldfish have three-second memories is repeated so often that it has become a fact in popular telling. Experiments with trained fish show them returning to a feeding site weeks later. The repetition of the claim, not the evidence, explains its persistence.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To challenge a widely repeated claim by pointing to contrary evidence.
wrongs: To explain how to train a goldfish to feed on cue.
To confirm that goldfish memory lasts only seconds.
To describe the anatomy of the goldfish brain.
why: Training is mentioned as evidence, not as instruction.
The passage contradicts the three-second claim.
Anatomy is never discussed.
items.explanation: The passage sets a popular claim against experimental evidence and explains its persistence.

items.passage: A weaver preparing a warp winds hundreds of threads onto a beam, keeping each at even tension. If one thread is tighter, it pulls the cloth out of shape later. The preparation is slow and invisible in the finished fabric, which is why it is easy to skimp and expensive to get wrong.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain why an invisible preparatory step matters to the final product.
wrongs: To describe the visible pattern of a finished cloth.
To argue that warp preparation can safely be skipped.
To compare two kinds of loom in detail.
why: The step's invisibility is the point.
Skimping is described as costly.
Looms are not compared here.
items.explanation: The passage connects an unseen preparation to a visible consequence.

items.passage: Some seeds remain dormant for decades even when conditions seem right. Scarification, whether by heat, abrasion or passage through an animal, can break that dormancy. The seed is not waiting passively; it is holding a lock that only particular events can open.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes an observation, illustrates it with examples, and closes with a comparison.
wrongs: It presents a chronological history of seed science.
It argues that dormancy is simply a passive waiting period.
It lists the chemical steps of germination in order.
why: No historical sequence is offered.
The final sentence rejects pure passivity.
Chemical steps are not given.
items.explanation: Observation, examples, then the lock metaphor shape the passage.

items.passage: An acoustic engineer testing a lecture hall found that speech was clear in the front rows but muddled at the back. The ceiling reflected sound back to the front while the rear received echoes from a flat wall. Adding curved diffusers at the rear changed the pattern without adding amplification.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a problem, identifies its cause, and reports a solution.
wrongs: It compares two halls and finds both equally clear.
It lists materials used in hall construction.
It argues that amplification is the only solution.
why: Only one hall is discussed.
Materials are incidental.
The solution avoids amplification.
items.explanation: Problem, cause and remedy structure the paragraph.

items.passage: A river that once meandered across a floodplain was straightened for navigation. The shortened channel carried water away faster, which deepened the bed and lowered the water table beside it. Farmland that had relied on the high water table dried, and the river began to cut downward rather than spread sideways.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It traces a chain of consequences that followed a single alteration.
wrongs: It compares two rivers and ranks their water quality.
It describes the construction of a navigation lock.
It argues that straightening a river has no downstream effects.
why: One river is followed.
No lock construction is described.
Consequences are the subject of the passage.
items.explanation: The paragraph moves from straightening to deepening to a lowered water table and dried farmland.

items.passage: A museum label once told visitors that a wooden mask was used in ceremonies. No record supported the claim. When the catalog was revised, the label was replaced with a note that the mask's use is unknown and that the wood dates to the twelfth century. The absence of evidence became part of the display.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To show how acknowledging missing evidence can improve an exhibit.
wrongs: To describe the carving techniques used on the mask.
To prove that the mask was used in ceremonies.
To explain how wooden objects are dated by museums.
why: Carving is not described.
The passage says the ceremony claim lacked support.
Dating is mentioned but not explained.
items.explanation: The revision turns an unsupported claim into an honest label.

items.passage: Two methods exist for measuring a forest's carbon. One counts every tree in sample plots and estimates the rest. The other uses laser scanning from an aircraft to map canopy height. Plot counts are accurate but slow; scanning is fast but needs calibration against plots. Neither stands alone.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It compares two methods, names the limits of each, and concludes that they depend on one another.
wrongs: It recommends abandoning plot counts in favor of scanning.
It describes a single method in step-by-step detail.
It argues that forest carbon cannot be measured.
why: Plot counts are needed for calibration.
Two methods are compared.
Measurement is described as possible.
items.explanation: The contrast and the calibration requirement produce the joint conclusion.

items.passage: A bell is rung once and the sound continues for many seconds. A listener hears a fundamental note plus weaker tones above it. The shape of the bell determines which of those tones are strong, and shifting one part of the profile can make a bell sound bright or dull without changing its fundamental pitch.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain how a bell's shape shapes its tone beyond the fundamental note.
wrongs: To describe the metal alloy used in bell casting.
To argue that a bell produces only one tone.
To explain how bell ringers time their strokes.
why: Alloy is not mentioned.
The passage describes multiple tones.
Ringing technique is not discussed.
items.explanation: The passage links profile shape to the strength of upper tones.

items.passage: Coastal dunes form when wind carries sand inland until vegetation slows it. The plants trap grains, and the dune grows upward. A single storm can cut the dune back, but the roots usually survive. The dune is therefore built slowly and destroyed quickly, a pattern that shapes how coastlines are managed.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains a formation process, notes a countervailing force, and draws a management implication.
wrongs: It tells the history of one particular coastline.
It argues that storms build dunes faster than vegetation does.
It lists the plant species found on dunes.
why: No specific coastline is followed.
Storms cut dunes back.
Species are not listed.
items.explanation: Growth, storm damage and management follow one another.

items.passage: Every year the same lake freezes later than it did a century ago. Records kept by a monastery note the first day of ice each winter. The series is not continuous, but the trend survives the gaps. A record kept for another purpose has become evidence for a changing climate.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To show how an incidental historical record can document long-term change.
wrongs: To describe the physics of lake freezing in detail.
To argue that the monastery records are useless.
To compare two lakes and explain their differences.
why: The physics is not the subject.
The records are presented as valuable.
Only one lake is discussed.
items.explanation: The final sentence states the reinterpretation of an old record.

items.passage: A chef testing a new oven found that the same recipe produced different results on different shelves. The top shelf browned too quickly, the bottom stayed pale. The chef rotated the trays halfway through and the variation fell. The oven's heat was uneven, and the method had been hiding it.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It reports observations, describes a fix, and explains what the observations revealed.
wrongs: It argues that oven shelves make no difference.
It lists the ingredients of the recipe.
It compares two ovens made by different manufacturers.
why: Shelf position is the variable.
Ingredients are not listed.
One oven is tested.
items.explanation: Observation, remedy and diagnosis form the sequence.

items.passage: Some desert plants open their pores at night rather than during the day. The cooler air reduces water loss, and the plant stores the carbon it takes in until daylight. The strategy trades a slower process for a much smaller water bill, which matters where rain is rare.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain how a night-time strategy reduces water loss in dry conditions.
wrongs: To describe how desert plants store water in their leaves.
To argue that opening pores at midday is more efficient.
To compare desert plants with rainforest species.
why: Storage of water is not described.
Midday opening would increase loss.
No rainforest comparison appears.
items.explanation: The passage links timing, temperature and water loss.

items.passage: A clockmaker adjusts a pendulum's length to change its period. A longer pendulum swings more slowly; a shorter one swings faster. Temperature matters too, because metal expands in warmth. Precision clocks therefore use alloys that change little with heat, or compensate with a second metal that expands in the opposite direction.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It states a basic relationship, introduces a complication, and describes two responses to it.
wrongs: It narrates the invention of the pendulum clock.
It argues that temperature has no effect on clocks.
It lists the parts of a clock in the order they are assembled.
why: No invention narrative appears.
Temperature is the complication.
No assembly order is given.
items.explanation: The period-length relation, thermal expansion, and two compensations build the paragraph.

items.passage: A farmer plants a cover crop after harvest. The roots hold soil through winter rains, and the plants add organic matter when they are turned in. The field looks idle, but the cover crop is working. Yield in the following season often rises even though nothing was harvested in between.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain the unseen benefits of a crop grown between harvests.
wrongs: To describe how to harvest a cover crop for profit.
To argue that bare soil is better for yields.
To compare two fertiliser brands.
why: Nothing is harvested from the cover crop.
Bare soil is the contrast case.
No brands are compared.
items.explanation: The passage explains what the cover crop does while looking idle.

items.passage: The first tests of a new vaccine measure immune response, not protection. A later trial follows thousands of people to see who becomes ill. The two stages answer different questions, and a strong immune response in the first does not guarantee success in the second. Reading the first result as a verdict is a common error.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It distinguishes two stages, explains what each measures, and warns against conflating them.
wrongs: It describes the manufacturing process of a vaccine.
It argues that early trials are unnecessary.
It reports the results of a completed field trial.
why: Manufacturing is not described.
Early trials are presented as one stage.
No results are reported.
items.explanation: The paragraph separates the two questions and names the mistake of merging them.

items.passage: A stone arch bridge carries load by compression. Each block pushes against its neighbors, and the curve directs the force into the abutments. The bridge can stand for centuries because the material is strong in compression. It fails when water scours the foundation and the abutments move, not because the stone crumbles.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains the structural principle and then names the usual cause of failure.
wrongs: It compares stone and steel bridges and prefers steel.
It describes the construction sequence of a bridge.
It argues that arches carry load in tension.
why: No steel comparison appears.
Construction order is not given.
The passage specifies compression.
items.explanation: The principle of compression is followed by scour as the failure mode.

items.passage: An archive received a box of letters with no catalog. A conservator noted the paper, ink and postmarks before anyone read them. The postmarks placed the letters in three decades; the ink identified two writers. Reading came last, after the physical evidence had narrowed the possibilities.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It narrates a sequence in which physical analysis precedes reading.
wrongs: It argues that letters should be read before being examined.
It lists the contents of the box in detail.
It describes how paper is manufactured.
why: Reading comes last in the passage.
Contents are summarized, not listed.
Manufacture is not discussed.
items.explanation: The order of steps is the structure the question asks about.

items.passage: A tidal flat looks uniform from a distance. Up close it holds channels, pools and patches of mud of different grain sizes. Each patch drains at a different rate, so the animals living in them experience different periods of exposure. A single square meter can contain several distinct habitats.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To show how small-scale variation creates distinct habitats on a seemingly uniform flat.
wrongs: To describe the tides that cover a flat twice a day.
To argue that grain size has no effect on drainage.
To list the species found on tidal flats.
why: Tide timing is not the subject.
Grain size is tied to drainage.
Species are mentioned generally.
items.explanation: The contrast between distant and close views carries the point.

items.passage: A baker's starter failed after a move to a new city. The flour was different, and so was the water. Replacing the flour restored the rise within a week, which suggested that the water was not the problem. The starter had been selective about its food all along.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a problem, tests one cause, and draws a conclusion from the result.
wrongs: It compares two cities and their baking traditions.
It argues that water quality never affects baking.
It lists the steps for making a starter from scratch.
why: No traditions are compared.
Water is ruled out only after the flour test.
No recipe is given.
items.explanation: The flour swap isolates the cause and produces the conclusion.

items.passage: A lighthouse's beam is narrow because a wide beam spreads its light too thin to be seen far. Rotating the beam sweeps the horizon, so a distant ship sees a flash rather than a steady glow. The flash pattern identifies the lighthouse, which is why each station has a different interval.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains a design choice, describes its effect, and states a further function of that effect.
wrongs: It narrates the construction of a lighthouse tower.
It argues that a wide beam is easier to see at sea.
It compares two lighthouses of different heights.
why: Construction is not described.
A wide beam spreads light too thin.
Heights are not compared.
items.explanation: Narrow beam, rotation and identifying flash build on one another.

items.passage: A museum once displayed a bronze horse without its stand because the stand was thought to be a later addition. Analysis of the metal showed the stand and the horse were cast together. The display was changed, and the label now explains that the two parts belong to one object.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To show how material analysis corrected an assumption about an object's parts.
wrongs: To describe the process of casting bronze.
To argue that museum labels are never revised.
To compare two bronze horses from different museums.
why: Casting technique is not explained.
A revision is the subject.
One object is discussed.
items.explanation: The passage contrasts an old assumption with the analysis that overturned it.

items.passage: A floodplain is not wasted land. When a river overtops its banks, the water slows and drops sediment that renews the soil. The same flood that damages a road may improve a field. Building levees everywhere removes the benefit along with the risk, which is why some rivers are now reconnected to their floodplains.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It challenges a common view, explains a benefit, and describes a policy response.
wrongs: It argues that levees are the only sensible flood policy.
It describes the geology of a river delta.
It lists the costs of flooding without mentioning benefits.
why: Levees are presented as removing a benefit.
Delta geology is not described.
Benefits are central to the passage.
items.explanation: The opening reframing leads to the sediment benefit and the reconnection policy.

items.passage: A new telescope's mirror is made of many hexagonal segments. Each segment is adjusted by actuators so that the whole surface behaves as one curve. A single large mirror would be too heavy to launch, so the design trades complexity on the ground for a lighter payload in orbit.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains a design, describes how it works, and states the trade-off that motivated it.
wrongs: It describes the launch sequence of a rocket.
It argues that a single large mirror is easier to launch.
It compares the images from two telescopes.
why: No launch sequence appears.
A single mirror is too heavy.
No images are compared.
items.explanation: Segment design, actuation and the launch-weight trade-off structure the passage.

items.passage: A seed catalog lists a tomato as resistant to a disease. Resistance does not mean immunity: the plant may still show symptoms under heavy pressure. Gardeners who read the label as a guarantee are disappointed, though the variety may still outperform others in the same bed.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To clarify a term that is easily misread as a stronger promise than it is.
wrongs: To describe how to grow tomatoes from seed.
To argue that resistant varieties never show symptoms.
To compare two tomato varieties for flavour.
why: Growing instructions are absent.
Symptoms can still appear.
Flavour is not discussed.
items.explanation: The passage defines resistance against a common misreading.

items.passage: A choral conductor asks singers to breathe in the same place in a phrase. The instruction is not about stamina. A shared breath makes the consonants land together, which is what the audience hears as precision. The technique is therefore about ensemble rather than endurance.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It states an instruction, rejects an obvious explanation, and gives the real one.
wrongs: It describes the history of choral music.
It argues that singers should breathe whenever they choose.
It explains how to train a solo voice.
why: No history is given.
Shared breathing is the instruction.
The focus is ensemble, not solo training.
items.explanation: The passage moves from instruction to rejected reason to the ensemble explanation.

items.passage: A concrete path cracks because it is restrained at the edges while the slab expands in heat. The crack relieves the stress at one point but concentrates it at the ends. A line of joints cut across the path gives the concrete places to move, so the cracks form where they were planned instead of randomly.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains a failure, describes how it propagates, and presents a design that controls it.
wrongs: It compares two kinds of concrete and ranks their strength.
It argues that joints make cracking worse.
It describes the mixing of a concrete batch.
why: No strength ranking appears.
Joints control where cracks form.
Mixing is not discussed.
items.explanation: Cause, propagation and control joints form the sequence.

items.passage: A historian reading a merchant's ledger noticed that the same cargo was recorded twice, once on departure and once on arrival. The two entries differ by a small amount, which probably reflects loss in transit. Such gaps, collected across many voyages, can estimate how much cargo never reached port.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a detail in a source and explains how that detail can be used at scale.
wrongs: It narrates a single voyage from departure to arrival.
It argues that ledgers are too unreliable to use.
It compares two merchants and their profits.
why: No voyage narrative is given.
The ledger is used, not dismissed.
One merchant is discussed.
items.explanation: A small discrepancy becomes a method when aggregated over many records.

items.passage: Some spiders build webs that reflect ultraviolet light. Insects see ultraviolet, so the web appears as a bright pattern to them while remaining nearly invisible to birds that might tear through it. The silk is not decorative; it is tuned to the vision of a particular audience.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain how a web's appearance is shaped by the vision of different animals.
wrongs: To describe how spiders spin silk threads.
To argue that birds are attracted to ultraviolet webs.
To compare the strength of two kinds of spider silk.
why: Spinning is not described.
Birds see the web as nearly invisible.
Strength is not compared.
items.explanation: The UV reflection is explained by what insects and birds can see.

items.passage: A town's water supply came from a spring above the town. The pipe ran downhill, so no pump was needed, but the pressure at the top of the hill was too low for firefighting. A second tank halfway up solved the problem by holding water at a height that gave pressure without a pump.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a system, names a shortcoming, and explains the remedy.
wrongs: It compares two towns and their water supplies.
It argues that pumps are always necessary.
It describes the construction of a spring house.
why: One town is discussed.
The solutions avoid pumps.
No spring house is described.
items.explanation: Gravity feed, weak pressure uphill, and a mid-level tank form the sequence.

items.passage: A paper was retracted after readers found that two figures were identical. The authors said the duplication was an error in assembling the manuscript. The journal's notice did not decide intent, only that the published record could no longer be relied on. Correction and misconduct are separate questions.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It reports an event, notes the authors' explanation, and distinguishes two issues the notice leaves separate.
wrongs: It argues that every retraction proves misconduct.
It describes how to assemble figures for publication.
It compares two journals and their retraction policies.
why: The passage separates correction from misconduct.
Figure assembly is mentioned but not explained.
One journal is discussed.
items.explanation: The final sentence draws the distinction the notice preserves.

items.passage: A beekeeper inspects a hive less often in winter. Opening the hive releases heat the colony has stored, and the bees must spend energy replacing it. A quick check may cost less than a cold night. The timing of an inspection is therefore a calculation, not a habit.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a practice and explains the cost that justifies it.
wrongs: It describes how bees make honey.
It argues that hives should be opened daily in winter.
It compares two species of bee.
why: Honey making is not described.
The passage recommends less frequent inspection.
One species is discussed.
items.explanation: The heat cost explains why inspections are rationed.

items.passage: A geologist found shells on a mountain top. The shells are marine, and the rock around them formed under water. The explanation is not that the sea once reached this height, but that the rock was lifted. Uplift is slow, which is why the shells remain intact rather than being crushed.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It poses an observation, rejects one explanation, and supplies another with supporting detail.
wrongs: It narrates a climb to a mountain summit.
It argues that the shells were carried up by birds.
It compares two mountain ranges.
why: No climb is described.
Birds are not mentioned.
One location is discussed.
items.explanation: The observation, rejected sea-level explanation and uplift account form the structure.

items.passage: A violin maker chooses wood for how it rings when tapped. A plate that rings too long sounds hollow under the bow; one that dies quickly sounds thin. The maker removes wood from the edges until the tap tone falls into a range learned from experience rather than measured on a scale.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain a judgement made by ear rather than by measurement.
wrongs: To describe the chemical treatment of violin varnish.
To argue that tap tone is irrelevant to violin sound.
To compare two famous violin makers.
why: Varnish is not discussed.
Tap tone is central.
No makers are compared.
items.explanation: The passage contrasts an experienced ear with a measured scale.

items.passage: A long drought exposed a submerged bridge in a reservoir. The bridge was built before the valley was flooded and had been underwater for sixty years. Its piers were intact, but the deck had sagged where water had entered the joints. The reservoir's low level turned a hidden structure into a visible record of its own construction.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It begins with a chance event and uses it to describe what the revealed structure shows.
wrongs: It argues that the bridge should never have been flooded.
It describes the engineering of reservoir dams.
It lists the materials used in bridge piers.
why: No judgement about flooding is offered.
Dams are not described.
Materials are not listed.
items.explanation: The drought is the occasion; the bridge's condition is the content.

items.passage: A museum's textile gallery dims its lights. Dyes fade in proportion to the light they receive, and a year of bright display can do more damage than a century in a drawer. Visitors sometimes complain about the gloom, but the alternative is the gradual disappearance of the objects they came to see.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It explains a policy, gives its rationale, and acknowledges a cost.
wrongs: It argues that bright lighting preserves textiles.
It describes the manufacture of natural dyes.
It compares two museums and their visitor numbers.
why: Light causes fading.
Dye manufacture is not described.
Visitor numbers are not compared.
items.explanation: Dim lighting, the fading mechanism and the visitor complaint complete the structure.

items.passage: A new bridge was built beside the old one rather than on its site. Keeping the old bridge open during construction meant traffic never stopped, but it also meant the new structure had to fit a narrower corridor. The builders accepted the constraint because the alternative was months of closure.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a decision and explains the trade-off that justified it.
wrongs: It compares the cost of two bridges in detail.
It narrates the failure of the old bridge.
It argues that road closures are always preferable.
why: No cost figures are given.
The old bridge stayed open.
Closures are the alternative that was avoided.
items.explanation: The siting decision and its traffic trade-off are the passage's content.

items.passage: A seed's size limits how far the wind can carry it. Small, winged seeds travel far but carry little stored food, so a seedling must establish quickly. Large seeds land near the parent but have reserves to survive shade. The trade-off shapes which species colonise open ground and which persist in closed forest.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It states a constraint, contrasts two strategies, and draws a consequence for where species grow.
wrongs: It describes the anatomy of a seed in detail.
It argues that large seeds travel farther than small ones.
It lists the animals that disperse seeds.
why: Anatomy is not the subject.
Small winged seeds travel farther.
No animals are listed.
items.explanation: Size, dispersal and establishment lead to the habitat conclusion.

items.passage: An archaeologist found a hearth with ash, burnt bone and a ring of stones. The stones were not local. Analysis matched them to a riverbed two days' walk away. The hearth therefore records not only a fire but a decision to carry heavy material to a place where it was wanted.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It presents evidence, links it to a distant source, and infers deliberate behavior.
wrongs: It narrates a journey to a riverbed.
It argues that the stones arrived by natural transport.
It compares two hearths from different sites.
why: The journey is inferred, not narrated.
The analysis ties the stones to the riverbed.
One hearth is discussed.
items.explanation: Evidence, provenance and inference about effort form the structure.

items.passage: A textile printer tests a dye on a scrap before committing a whole bolt. The scrap is washed, dried and exposed to light in conditions harsher than ordinary use. If the color survives that, the bolt is printed. The test is a small, deliberate failure used to prevent a large one.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain why a small destructive test protects a larger investment.
wrongs: To describe how dye is extracted from plants.
To argue that testing scraps is a waste of material.
To compare two printing machines.
why: Extraction is not described.
The test prevents loss.
No machines are compared.
items.explanation: The last sentence states the logic of the sample test.

items.passage: A city planted trees along a new road. Within five years, half had died, mostly in the pits cut into compacted ground. The failures were not caused by drought or disease but by roots unable to spread beyond the pit. Later plantings broke the surrounding compaction before planting.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It reports an outcome, rules out two explanations, and identifies the real cause.
wrongs: It narrates the construction of the road.
It argues that tree pits are the best place to plant.
It lists the species of trees planted.
why: Road construction is incidental.
Pits are the problem.
Species are not listed.
items.explanation: Mortality, rejected causes and compaction form the paragraph.

items.passage: A stone tool's edge dulls at a rate that depends on what it cuts. Microscopic wear on a blade can distinguish hide from wood from bone. An archaeologist can therefore infer what a tool was used for without finding the material it worked on. The evidence is the surface, not the residue.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To explain how wear patterns on a tool reveal its past use.
wrongs: To describe how stone tools are made.
To argue that tools cannot reveal their function.
To compare two archaeological sites.
why: Manufacture is not described.
Function is the subject.
No sites are compared.
items.explanation: The passage explains wear analysis and its inferential reach.

items.passage: A wick must be the right size for a candle. Too small and the flame starves; too large and it smokes, leaving soot on the glass. Candle makers match wick diameter to the wax and the container. A wick that works in one candle may fail in another of the same height.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a requirement, gives failure modes, and concludes that the choice is specific.
wrongs: It narrates the history of candle making.
It argues that one wick size suits every candle.
It describes how wax is refined.
why: No history is given.
The passage says a wick can fail in another candle.
Wax refining is not discussed.
items.explanation: Requirement, failure modes and the specificity conclusion build the text.

items.passage: An island's birds were larger than their mainland relatives. With no ground predators, large size was not a liability. When people introduced rats, the largest ground-nesting species vanished first. Size had been an advantage that became a disadvantage in one generation.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It describes a pattern, explains its original cause, and shows how a new factor reversed it.
wrongs: It compares two islands and their climates.
It argues that island birds are always smaller than mainland birds.
It lists the predators introduced to the island.
why: Only one island is discussed.
The passage says the birds were larger.
One predator is named, not listed as a group.
items.explanation: Advantage, explanation and reversal form the arc.

items.passage: A manuscript's margins are wide because the skin was expensive and the scribe planned them. Ruling lines left faint grooves that are still visible. The widths are consistent across a whole scriptorium, which suggests a standard rather than an individual choice. The page layout is therefore evidence of workshop practice.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?
items.correct: To show how a page's physical features can reveal how it was produced.
wrongs: To describe the animals whose skin was used.
To argue that margins were always random.
To compare two scribes and their handwriting.
why: Animals are not described.
The widths are consistent.
Handwriting is not compared.
items.explanation: Margins and ruling grooves are read as evidence of workshop standards.

items.passage: A wing's shape produces lift because air moves faster over the curved upper surface. That faster air has lower pressure, and the difference pushes the wing upward. The explanation is often simplified as a longer path over the top, but the length of the path is not what matters. Pressure, not distance, does the work.
items.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.correct: It states a mechanism, corrects a popular version of it, and names the real cause.
wrongs: It describes the history of aviation in order.
It argues that wing shape has no effect on lift.
It lists the forces acting on a paper plane.
why: No history is given.
Shape produces lift in the passage.
No forces are listed.
items.explanation: The passage presents the pressure difference and corrects the equal-transit explanation.
